bib.title: Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners", Yasunaga, Chen, Li, Pasupat, Leskovec, Liang, Chi, Zhou (Google DeepMind, Stanford). ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2310.01714v3, Mar 2024).

COVERAGE: All 25 pages, 96,753 chars, read (main text, limitations, Tables 1-8, appendices A-D; the reference list only skimmed; D.2-D.4 full example outputs skimmed). Extraction was clean. Table 1 header text is slightly jumbled (column order); I resolved it via the 5 values per row.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Analogical prompting (the model self-generates relevant exemplars, optionally preceded by a tutorial, then solves the problem, all in ONE prompt) beats 0-shot CoT and fixed few-shot CoT on average.
  number: +4% average accuracy gain
  setup: GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces, 5 BIG-Bench tasks; GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM2
  quote: "achieving an average accuracy gain of +4%"
  where: p.2 (Intro)
- Math (Table 1). Self-generated exemplars vs 5-shot CoT vs 0-shot CoT. GSM8K: GPT-3.5-turbo 77.8 / 76.7 / 75.8; text-davinci-003 61.0 / 54.0 / 50.3; PaLM2 81.7 / 80.7 / 78.2. MATH: GPT-3.5-turbo 37.3 / 34.9 / 33.9; PaLM2 34.8 / 34.3 / 29.8. Temperature 0.
  quote: "Ours: Self-generated Exemplars 77.8% 61.0% † 81.7% 37.3% 34.8%" ; "5-shot CoT 76.7% 54.0% 80.7% 34.9% 34.3%"
  where: p.7. Caveat: for text-davinci-003 the paper adds "For text-davinci models, we use an in-context demonstration of how to generate exemplars."
  Gains on GSM8K with chat models are about 1 point; the largest gains are on MATH and davinci.
- Gains depend on model scale. With small models, labeled few-shot CoT wins; self-generation only wins from text-davinci-002 up. GSM8K (Table 4), columns curie-001 / davinci-001 / davinci-002 / davinci-003: 0-shot 2/6/13/14; 0-shot CoT 2/6/22/50; 5-shot fixed CoT 2/10/43/54; 5-shot retrieved CoT 3/11/47/57; ours 2/9/48/61.
  quote: "When using smaller-scale LLMs (text-curie-001 and text-davinci-001), few-shot CoT leveraging labeled exemplars exhibits superior performance compared to ours. However, as the LLMs are scaled up to text-davinci-002 and text-davinci-003, our method outperforms few-shot CoT."
  where: p.8-9 (6.4). Even at davinci-002 the margin over retrieved CoT is 48 vs 47.
- Generated vs retrieved exemplars. Retrieval (Sentence-BERT, top-5 by cosine from the train set) is more reliable and better for small models. Generation is better for larger models.
  quote: "Our method outperforms the retrieved CoT with larger-scale LLMs, such as text-davinci-003." ; "Conversely, with smaller-scale LLMs, the retrieved CoT performs better, and self-generation fails to produce useful or valid exemplars."
  where: p.8-9 (6.3)
- Code generation (Codeforces, Table 2). Self-generated knowledge (tutorial) plus exemplars gives extra gain over exemplars alone. GPT-3.5-turbo-16k Acc@1/Acc@10: 0-shot 8/24; 0-shot CoT 9/27; 3-shot CoT 11/27; exemplars 13/25; knowledge+exemplars 15/29. GPT-4: 16/30; 16/29; 17/31; 17/32; 19/37. GPT-3.5 with the method (15%) is close to GPT-4 0-shot (16%).
  quote: "Ours: Self-generated Knowledge + Exemplars 15% 29% 19% 37%" ; "GPT3.5-turbo achieves competitive performance with GPT4, with a 15% Acc@1 compared to GPT4's 16% Acc@1."
  setup: temperature 0.7, 10 samples per problem. Exemplars alone on GPT-3.5 get Acc@10 25%, below 0-shot CoT's 27% and 3-shot CoT's 27%.
  where: p.7
- Knowledge ordering matters slightly. Knowledge before exemplars: 15/29. After: 14/27 (GPT-3.5-turbo, Codeforces).
  quote: "Ours: Self-generate knowledge before exemplars 15% 29%"
  where: p.17 (Table 7)
- BIG-Bench (Table 3, GPT-3.5-turbo, temperature 0, 3 exemplars). Columns word sorting / logical deduction 5 objects / temporal sequences / colored objects / formal fallacies. Ours 75.2/41.6/57.6/68.0/58.8. 3-shot CoT 68.4/36.4/58.0/62.0/55.6. 0-shot CoT 67.6/35.2/44.8/61.6/55.6. Only temporal sequences is below manual 3-shot (57.6 vs 58.0).
  quote: "Ours: Self-generated Exemplars 75.2% 41.6% 57.6% 68.0% 58.8%"
  where: p.7
- Number of self-generated exemplars K (GPT-3.5-turbo), GSM8K / MATH: K=1 76.1/34.8; K=2 77.0/36.7; K=3 77.5/37.3; K=4 77.3/37.0; K=5 77.8/37.1. Best at 3 or 5.
  quote: "When K =1, the LLM underperforms due to excessive reliance on a single exemplar generated. When K ≥ 3, the LLM demonstrates consistent performance"
  where: p.9 (Table 5)
  The prompt instruction says K = 3 to 5 works best. Used K=5 for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH/BIG-Bench/Codeforces.
- Asking for DIVERSE exemplars helps (GPT-3.5-turbo): GSM8K 75.9 to 77.8, MATH 35.2 to 37.3.
  quote: "Ours: Non-diverse exemplars 75.9% 35.2%" / "Ours: Diverse exemplars 77.8% 37.3%"
  where: p.17 (Table 6). Text: "some LLMs have a tendency to repetitively generate identical problems, which can be misleading"
- Self-consistency stacks with it: GSM8K 77.8 to 85.3, MATH 37.3 to 46.0.
  quote: "Ours + Self-consistency 85.3% 46.0%"
  where: p.17 (Table 8). The number of samples is not stated in what I read.
- Single-pass generation is about as good as sampling exemplars independently and re-prompting. No numbers are given.
  quote: "our current single-pass prompt approach achieves comparable performance and offers greater convenience"
  where: p.4
- Error analysis (50 correct and 50 incorrect on GSM8K+MATH). Correct: 35/50 relevant and correct exemplars, 9/50 relevant but wrong solutions, 6/50 irrelevant. Incorrect: 28/50 exemplars fine but the model still failed (12 generalization gap, 8 overreliance on specific exemplars, 8 other); 12/50 relevant but wrong; 10/50 irrelevant. Note that 9/50 correct answers came from exemplars with wrong solutions.
  quote: "(35/50) Generated exemplars are relevant and correct"
  where: p.9 (6.6)

LIMITS
- Authors concede: more output tokens and more inference compute than 0-shot or 0-shot CoT. Versus few-shot CoT: "we use fewer input tokens and more output tokens." Self-generation fails if the model is weak or has not seen related problems, so it is "better suited for stronger or larger-scale LLMs". It is prompt-sensitive (Jiang et al., 2020).
- Not shown by the paper: GSM8K gains on chat models are small (about 1 point) and no variance, seeds or significance tests are reported. Codeforces is only 50 level-A problems from 2023 (collected Jan-Aug 2023), run twice and averaged (App. B), so the Acc@1 differences of 1-2 points are within noise. Models are 2023-era (GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4 June-Sept 2023, PaLM2, text-davinci). No reasoning models, and no comparison with modern strong baselines. The few-shot baseline uses 5 shots (GSM8K/MATH) or 3 hand-written (others). BIG-Bench was tested only on GPT-3.5-turbo. Exemplar correctness is not verified, so the generated exemplars can be wrong. The self-consistency sample count is not in the text I read.
- The paper does not compare against "generic" dynamic exemplar selection beyond Sentence-BERT retrieval.

BUILDS ON
Few-shot CoT (Wei et al. 2022b); 0-shot CoT (Kojima et al. 2022); in-context learning (Brown et al. 2020); retrieval-based CoT (Zhang et al. 2022b, Auto-CoT; Shum et al. 2023); recitation (Sun et al. 2022); self-generated ICL (Kim et al. 2022); self-prompting (Li et al. 2022a); self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022); least-to-most (Zhou et al. 2022); Polya "How to solve it" (2004) and analogical reasoning in psychology (Vosniadou & Ortony 1989; Gentner 1983).

CODE (prompt templates, verbatim)
- p.3-4, generic exemplar template:
  "# Problem: [ x]
  # Relevant problems: Recall three relevant and distinct problems. For each problem, describe it and explain the solution.
  # Solve the initial problem:"
- p.4, knowledge add-on: "# Tutorial: Identify core concepts in the problem and provide a tutorial."
- p.17 (App. D.1), math prompt: "Your task is to tackle mathematical problems. When presented with a math problem, recall relevant problems as examples. Afterward, proceed to solve the initial problem. ... ## Relevant Problems: Recall three examples of math problems that are relevant to the initial problem. Note that your problems should be distinct from each other and from the initial problem (e.g., involving different numbers and names). For each problem: - After "Q: ", describe the problem - After "A: ", explain the solution and enclose the ultimate answer in \boxed{}. ## Solve the Initial Problem: ..."
- p.6 (Fig. 3), Codeforces: "## Algorithms: Identify the core concepts or algorithms used to solve the problem. ## Tutorial: Write a tutorial about these algorithms. ## Example Problems: Provide three examples of relevant competitive programming problems that involve these algorithms. For each problem, describe the problem, explain the solution in detail, and then write the correct Python3 code. ## Python3 code to solve the original problem:"
- The paper says "#" headers help structure the output.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.2): 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, few-shot CoT and analogical prompting side by side on the same geometry problem. It shows fixed exemplars versus problem-tailored self-generated ones in one view.
- Fig. 2 (p.5): the actual MATH prompt and GPT-3.5 output (probability exemplars).
- Fig. 3 (p.6): Codeforces prompt with tutorial plus exemplars, with the generated prefix-product knowledge and code.
- Tables 1-4 and 7-8 hold the results (they are text tables, not figures).

PROBLEMS: No extraction faults beyond the garbled Table 1 header. No embedded instructions found in the text. The ledger or note files were not read, as the task did not require it; no files edited.
